Building a bridge between Google Photos and Wikimedia Commons is an excellent open-source project. However, you are beginning this at a critical transition point. Google is currently implementing major changes to its Photos APIs that fundamentally alter how third-party applications interact with user data.

Below is the verified, up-to-date technical guide for your architecture as of July 2026, incorporating the mandatory March 2025 API transition.

1. Google Photos APIs

  • Available APIs: The Google Photos Picker API (New) and the Google Photos Library API (Updated/Legacy).
  • Status:
    • Picker API: General Availability (GA). This is the recommended API for your use case.
    • Library API: Deprecated for general library access. As of March 31, 2025, it is restricted to "App-Created Content" only.
  • Is Library API still available? Yes, but its scope is now limited.
  • Functionality Remaining in Library API: You can only list, retrieve, or search for photos/videos that your specific application uploaded. You can still use it to upload new media to Google Photos.
  • Functionality Removed from Library API: You can no longer list the user's entire library, search across their library, or access shared albums/media not created by your app. These calls now return 403 PERMISSION_DENIED.
  • Picker API Recommendation: Yes. The Picker API is now the only way for a user to select existing photos from their personal library to share with your app.
  • Architectural Differences:
    • Library API: Provided programmatic, "silent" access to the full library (if authorized). The app drove the browsing experience.
    • Picker API: User-driven. Google hosts the selection UI. Your app creates a "session," the user picks specific photos in a Google-hosted window, and your app receives only the IDs for those specific items.

2. OAuth and Authentication

The Picker API uses a Session-based flow.

  • OAuth Scopes:
    • Required: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/photospicker.mediaitems.readonly (for picking).
    • Optional: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/photoslibrary.appendonly (if you want to allow users to upload back to Google Photos).
    • Deprecated: photoslibrary.readonly, photoslibrary.sharing, and the base photoslibrary scope (for general access).
  • Client Type for Toolforge: Web Application.
  • Localhost Restrictions: Google allows http://localhost for redirect URIs during development. However, for production (Toolforge), you must use https.
  • Refresh Tokens: Supported. To receive one, you must include access_type=offline and prompt=consent in your initial authorization request.
  • Token Validity:
    • Access Tokens: Fixed at 3,600 seconds (1 hour).
    • Refresh Tokens: Indefinite, unless the user revokes access or the token is inactive for 6 months. Note: In "Testing" mode, refresh tokens expire in 7 days.
  • Backend vs. Frontend: The OAuth flow should be initiated by the frontend, but the Access/Refresh tokens should be exchanged and stored on the FastAPI backend for security. The Picker session itself is created by the backend.

3. Google Cloud Project Setup

  1. Enable APIs: Enable "Google Photos Picker API" and "Google Photos Library API" in the API Library .
  2. OAuth Consent Screen:
    • User Type: External (since it's for any Google user).
    • Branding: Provide App Name, User Support Email, and Developer Contact. Note: Logos require brand verification to be visible.
    • Scopes: Add the photospicker.mediaitems.readonly scope.
  3. Publishing Status: Start in Testing. Add your email as a Test User. Move to Production to remove the 7-day token limit.
  4. Credentials:
    • Create OAuth 2.0 Client ID (Web application).
    • Authorized Redirect URIs: Add https://<your-tool-name>.toolforge.org/api/auth/callback and http://localhost:8000/api/auth/callback.
  5. IAM: No specific IAM permissions or Service Accounts are required for end-user auth; Google Photos APIs do not support Service Accounts.

4. Google Cloud CLI vs Console Support

Task Console UI gcloud CLI Terraform APIs
Enable APIs Yes Yes Yes Yes
Configure Consent Screen Yes No* No No
Create OAuth Client ID Yes No No No
Add Redirect URIs Yes No No No
Add Test Users Yes No No No
View Quotas Yes Yes No Yes

*Limited support via gcloud alpha for branding, but manual UI setup is recommended for OAuth.

5. Quotas and Limits

Limit Type Picker API (New) Library API (Legacy/Upload)
Daily Request Limit 100,000 per minute 10,000 per day
Media Byte Access 1,000,000 per minute 75,000 per day
File Size Limit N/A (Picking only) 200 MB (Photos) / 10 GB (Videos)
Session Lifetime Short-lived (Poll-based) N/A
  • Pricing: The Picker API and Library API are currently Free to use. There are no billing implications unless you exceed these generous quotas, which usually requires joining the Partner Program.

6. Security Best Practices

  • Secret Storage: Never store client secrets in React code or Git. Use Toolforge Environment Variables or a hidden config file on the Toolforge home directory.
  • Session Management: Use Server-side sessions (e.g., stored in a database or Redis). The backend should map a secure session cookie to the user's Google Refresh Token.
  • Cookies: Use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax (or Strict) cookies to store your app's session ID.
  • Picker Specifics: Always Delete the Picker session on your backend via the API once the media items are retrieved.

7. Toolforge Compatibility

  • Redirect URIs: Toolforge uses <tool>.toolforge.org. You must register this exact domain in your Google Cloud Console.
  • HTTPS: Toolforge provides HTTPS by default, which is mandatory for Google OAuth.
  • CORS: If your FastAPI backend and React frontend are on different subdomains, you must configure FastAPI's CORSMiddleware.
  • Domain Verification: Google requires you to verify ownership of your domain (e.g., via a TXT record or HTML file) before you can move your OAuth app to "Production" status. On Toolforge, this is usually done via an HTML file in your public_html or a specific FastAPI route.

8. Recommended Architecture

  1. Frontend (React/TS): Handles the "Login with Google" button. Receives the pickerUri from the backend and opens it in a new window/tab.
  2. Backend (FastAPI):
    • OAuth Handler: Exchanges the authorization code for tokens. Stores the Refresh Token in a database (e.g., Toolforge's MariaDB).
    • Picker Orchestrator: Calls sessions.create to get a pickerUri.
    • Poller/Webhook: Periodically checks session status or waits for the user to return.
  3. Upload Pipeline:
    • Once a photo is picked, the backend gets the baseUrl.
    • Backend streams the bytes directly from Google to Wikimedia Commons (to avoid storing large files on Toolforge).
  4. Error Handling: Implement Exponential Backoff for 429 (Rate Limit) errors.

9. Future-proofing

  • Library API Shutdown: If you were planning to "auto-sync" folders, that is no longer possible. The architecture must be interactive.
  • Identity Services: Use the Google Identity Services (GIS) library for the frontend, as older libraries (GSI/GAPI) are being phased out.
  • Scopes: Stick strictly to photospicker scopes. Do not use photoslibrary.readonly as it will break your app in March 2025.
